item.title: The Pursuit of Legacy May Be Burning Us Out
item.description:
Happiness

The Pursuit of Legacy May Be Burning Us Out

The case for being forgettable.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • Modern culture pressures us to turn hobbies into monetized brands, creating anxiety over leaving a legacy.
  • Cultivating a quiet ego shifts focus away from status toward pursuits that are intrinsically meaningful.
  • Releasing our grip on immortality allows us to enjoy the present moment without needing a permanent monument.

We all have that one thing that we love to do. Some people like baking, others like collecting records or dressing up like superheroes. For others, like Ed, it’s throwing boomerangs.

Ed belongs to a dedicated global community that takes the sport so seriously that its members recently competed in the World Boomerang Championships in Indonesia. Watching these competitors master a niche craft is remarkable. It takes baseline focus, hundreds of hours of practice, and dedication to the flight.

For most of us, though, throwing a boomerang starts as something far simpler: heading out to an open field, tossing a curved piece of wood into the air, and watching it carve a quiet arc through the sky before returning to your hand. It’s an invitation to just enjoy the moment.

In modern culture, enjoying a hobby for its own sake is rarely treated as enough. First comes the pressure to be great, then to record it, then to build an audience around it, and eventually to monetize it into a side hustle. But underlying all of this optimization is a deeper, more insidious anxiety: the modern obsession with leaving a legacy.

Someone (probably not Teddy Roosevelt) once said, “Comparison is the thief of joy.” While throwing with his boomerang community is a peak experience for Ed, he tries to learn from the true legends of the sport without expecting to imitate them. The key is not to be great but to be better.

For years, very few people knew of Ed’s interest in boomerangs. When he helped some students start a boomerang club and then reentered the competitive world, he became known (at least at his university) as the boomerang professor. It is part of his personal brand, whether he likes it or not (he’s okay with it). Sometimes we can’t help but be marked by what we love. Now, though, the pressure he feels to live up to the mark adds an unwelcome seriousness to a playful sport.

Why We Want to Be Remembered

What drives the desire to be remembered to create a legacy? Social psychologists point to Terror Management Theory (TMT); the idea that the inevitability of our death profoundly impacts our thoughts, behavior and motivation.

As a reaction to TMT, we create “immortality projects” in the hope some piece of us will survive after we are long gone. Our modern obsession with “hustle” and productivity helps drive this anxiety. Corporations add to this by reframing work as “legacy building" so we get caught up in trying to outrun our own mortality, which leads to burnout.

The Freedom of the "Quiet Ego"

What’s the alternative? Positive psychologists Heidi Wayment and Jack Bauer proposed a construct called the Quiet Ego.

A Quiet Ego isn’t focused on status-seeking, clout, or chasing likes, but it also doesn’t sacrifice self-worth. Instead, it has us step off the treadmill of constant self-promotion and focus on things that are intrinsically meaningful and motivating to us.

Studies show that people who cultivate a Quiet Ego enjoy higher psychological resilience, and deeper, more authentic self-compassion. They just enjoy the experience of doing them.

So how do we actually quiet the noise and build a life that feels deeply satisfying without needing to broadcast or immortalize it? It starts with unlearning the idea that quiet lives are wasted lives.

Practical Forgettability

If you're ready to drop the exhausting burden of needing to be "extraordinary," here are four concrete ways to practice the freedom of forgettability:

  • Treat Work as a Craft, Not an Identity: Lower the existential stakes of your career. You can do excellent, painstaking work today without demanding that your job title serve as your biography's opening line.
  • Embrace "Anonymous Impact": Practice doing good things like helping a colleague, fixing a broken system, supporting a cause without posting about it or needing your name attached to the donor list.
  • Reclaim the Freedom to Fail: When you aren't trying to build a permanent monument to yourself, mistakes are no longer existential threats. They’re just data points.
  • Cultivate "Quiet Hobbies": Keep at least one passion entirely unmonetized, unrecorded, and offline; your own private boomerang field that exists for your eyes only.

Releasing the Grip

In the physics of boomerang flight, everything depends on the release. If you hold on too tight, or throw it with a rigid, desperate grip, the aerodynamics fall apart and the boomerang plummets straight into the dirt. It only lifts, arcs, and returns when you let it go cleanly.

Maybe the ultimate act of quiet rebellion today is to reclaim the things we love simply because they bring us joy in the moment. Paint a picture no one will ever scroll past, master an instrument you only play when the house is empty, or bake a loaf of sourdough that gets eaten in ten minutes and never makes it onto an Instagram story.

You don't need a monument, an audience, or a global stage to justify your time on this planet. The worth of a life is measured by how fully you felt it while you were here.

Cheer for those who reach the global stage. Marvel at their focus and celebrate their niche mastery. But remember: you don't owe the world an extraordinary performance, a personal brand, or a slot in the history books.

Sometimes, throwing a boomerang into an empty field and watching it return to your hand is more than enough. Not because it’s going to change the world, but simply because, for a few quiet seconds, it felt wonderful to catch it.

Live your life, enjoy the flight while it lasts, and grant yourself the sweet, peaceful permission to be forgotten.

item.title: Stop Bankrolling Your Adult Child's Stuck Life
item.description:
Parenting

Stop Bankrolling Your Adult Child's Stuck Life

Why financial rescue often ends up financing the struggle you're trying to solve.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • Rescue money often substitutes for a hard conversation.
  • When there's no plan attached to the money, there's no reason for anything to change.
  • The goal is accountability, not punishment.

Back in 1973, Pink Floyd built an entire song around the strange hold that money has over us. He sang about how it can dominate a person's thinking, even when no one's talking about it out loud. Half a century later, I hear that same undertone in almost every session I have with parents of struggling adult children. Nobody wants to talk about the money, but it's always in the room.

Here are some examples from my parent coaching work (names changed here) of what I mean. A father named Roger told me he "just helped out a little" with his 27-year-old son, Jake's, rent—but this was for the ninth month in a row. A mother, Louisa, described covering her daughter, Lilly's, car payment "until she gets back on her feet," a phrase she's used for two straight years.

Neither parent set out to create dependency. Both did it out of love, but now they're bankrolling lives that aren't moving anywhere because the money has become the conversation. Let me make this clear. I am not opposed to parents financially helping their adult children. But when money becomes a stand-in for the honest, sometimes uncomfortable talk about what's actually keeping their adult child stuck, that's a big-time problem.

The Trap of Financial Rescue Without a Plan

This is the trap I want to name clearly: financial rescue, offered without structure, doesn't just fail to solve the problem—it often removes the very discomfort that would motivate change. If rent gets paid no matter what, there's no natural consequence nudging your son toward that job search. If the car payment always appears, there's no pressure prompting your daughter to budget. You haven't bought peace. You've bought more time inside the same stuck pattern.

None of this means parents should slam the door. I've watched that backfire just as badly as it has with parents whose adult children feel abandoned rather than challenged. Those adult children tend to spiral further, not straighten out. The answer isn't rescue or refusal. Rather, the key is the structure, presented with a mix of compassion and inspiration. A "yes, and here's what comes with it" instead of an unconditional bailout. This often means discussing a specific end date instead of "until you're back on your feet." A shared plan will go a long way toward helping, rather than you slipping into your first-responder uniform and reflexively sending money through an app that leaves you with only a hopeful shrug.

Sound Strategies Versus Creating More Dependency

I explore this dynamic in depth in my book, Mom, Dad, I Promise I'll Pay You Back, which examines how families can replace guilt-driven giving with boundary-supported support. The key is to provide strategies that actually move an adult child forward, rather than quietly financing their standstill.

For example, try this the next time a request for money comes in: instead of asking "how much do you need?", try "Let's figure out together what would actually move you forward. In reflecting on the pressures you're facing, what do you see as the next step?" It's a small shift in language, but it moves the entire conversation from rescue to partnership.

The Takeaway

Money may not buy happiness, as the old saying goes—but handed over the wrong way, it can quietly buy stagnation instead. The fix isn't a bigger wallet; it's a clearer, workable plan.
